content: Waveform refers to the specific shape and structure of a signal, such as a wave traveling through a solid, liquid, or gaseous medium. In many situations, the medium through which the wave propagates does not allow for a direct visual representation of the wave's form. In such cases, the term waveform is used to describe the shape of a graph that represents the variation of a quantity (such as amplitude) over time or distance. An oscilloscope, a specialized instrument, can be employed to visually display the waveform as a repeating image on a cathode-ray tube (CRT) or liquid crystal display (LCD) screen. Furthermore, the term waveform has been extended to describe the graphical representation of any variable quantity as it changes over time. Examples of Waveforms 1. Sine Wave: The sine wave is mathematically expressed as sin(2πt). Its amplitude varies according to a trigonometric sine function with respect to time. This waveform is smooth and continuous, making it fundamental in many physical and engineering applications. 2. Sawtooth Wave: The sawtooth wave is represented by the equation 2(t − floor(t)) − 1. Its shape resembles the teeth of a saw. This waveform is commonly used in time bases for display scanning and serves as a foundational waveform in subtractive synthesis. A sawtooth wave with a constant period contains both odd and even harmonics, which decrease in amplitude at a rate of −6 dB per octave. 3. Square Wave: The square wave can be mathematically described as saw(x) − saw(x − duty). It is widely used to represent digital information. A square wave with a constant period contains only odd harmonics, and their amplitudes decrease at a rate of −6 dB per octave. 4. Triangle Wave: The triangle wave is expressed as (t − 2 floor((t + 1)/2)) (−1)floor((t + 1)/2). It is essentially the integral of a square wave. This waveform contains only odd harmonics, but their amplitudes decrease more rapidly, at a rate of −12 dB per octave. Other types of waveforms, often referred to as composite waveforms, can be described as combinations of multiple sinusoidal waves or other fundamental basis functions. The Fourier series provides a mathematical framework for decomposing periodic waveforms into their constituent components. According to this principle, any periodic waveform can be represented as the sum of a fundamental frequency component and its harmonic components. Additionally, finite-energy non-periodic waveforms can be analyzed into sinusoidal components using the Fourier transform.
